standard.title: Texts take many forms
standard.description: understand that texts can take many forms such as signs, books and digital texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have interacted with texts in home and community settings. They have not yet been asked to consciously categorise and compare text forms, or to understand that form and purpose are connected.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify a range of text forms, explain what each is for, and recognise that the purpose of a text shapes its form — including that First Nations Australians' stories may be oral or image-based rather than print.

nodes.label: Texts are all around us
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that texts are present in many places and take different physical forms.
nodes.minimum_width: Name at least two different types of text seen in the world (e.g. a book and a sign).
nodes.typical_width: Identify texts in school, home and community settings across multiple forms: signs, books, digital texts, labels, instructions; recognise these as different types of text.
wider: Create a class collection or photo record of texts found in the school and local community, sorting them by form
Investigate texts in culturally diverse contexts — including community languages and First Nations Australian contexts — identifying forms that may not appear in school settings
nodes.hinge_reason: Without recognising that texts exist in multiple forms in the world, students cannot reason in Node 2 about why different forms serve different purposes — form-purpose reasoning requires having a repertoire of text forms to reason about.

response_modes.reason: Text form recognition must be reliable and broad before form-purpose reasoning can be applied. Practice identifying texts across multiple settings builds the necessary repertoire.

success_criteria: Student can name at least two different text forms encountered in everyday settings.
Student can distinguish a text from a non-text (e.g. a picture vs a labelled diagram).

nodes.label: Form follows purpose
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that different text forms exist because they serve different purposes — form and purpose are connected.
nodes.minimum_width: Match at least one text form to its purpose (e.g. a crossing sign tells you when it is safe to cross).
nodes.typical_width: Identify texts and explain what each is for; compare different ways information might be presented (e.g. on a sign vs in a set of instructions); identify similarities and differences in text forms.
wider: Compare how the same information (e.g. 'wash your hands') is presented in different forms — a sign, a set of written instructions, a picture — and discuss what each form is best for
Investigate how digital texts serve different purposes from print texts — exploring apps, websites and e-books alongside paper forms

response_modes.reason: Students may initially think that purpose and form are arbitrary — the misconception is that a text could be in any form. Multiple specific examples where form matches purpose (a crossing sign cannot be a novel) help consolidate the connection.

success_criteria: Student can explain why a particular text takes the form it does — connecting form to purpose.
Student can give an example of a text form that would not suit a particular purpose and explain why.

nodes.label: First Nations texts — oral and image-based forms
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise that texts can be oral and image-based — not only written — and that First Nations Australians' stories are examples of this.
nodes.minimum_width: Recognise that a story can be told through speech or images, not only through writing.
nodes.typical_width: Understand that many First Nations Australians' stories are oral narrations and cultural accounts that may be represented as or with images; identify examples of oral and image-based texts and discuss what form they take.
wider: Engage with First Nations Australian stories from multiple forms — oral, visual, digital and multimodal sources — and compare how each form presents the story
Discuss how oral and image-based texts have been transmitted across generations and why this matters for the communities that created them
Compare images in First Nations Australian texts with images in non-Indigenous picture books — exploring how images carry cultural meaning

response_modes.reason: The risk is that students form a 'texts are written' misconception — this node explicitly widens that schema. Multiple First Nations examples from different sources are needed to ensure the understanding generalises beyond a single example.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: This node has genuine richness: oral, visual, and multimodal First Nations texts offer substantive opportunities for cultural learning, media literacy, and understanding of how diverse communities create and transmit knowledge — well beyond what is needed to meet the descriptor.
success_criteria: Student can name at least one type of text that is not written and explain that it is still a text.
Student can identify a First Nations Australian text form and describe what form it takes.
Student can explain why not all texts are books or written texts.
